suite: Cornered by a serial killer who hurt my family, holding a weapon
nightmare: I’m backed into the corner of my childhood kitchen, the yellow light above the stove flickering, and he’s standing in the doorway with that same blank expression, the metal of the knife catching the light every time his hand twitches. I can smell blood and bleach and something rotten, and somewhere behind me I hear my family crying and choking, their voices muffled like they’re under water, while the floor feels sticky under my bare feet. He takes one slow step toward me and I can hear the scrape of his boots on the tile, my chest locking so tight I can’t scream, and all I can do is stare at the dark stains on his shirt and the weapon lifting in his hand. Right before he reaches me, I see over his shoulder that my family is lying motionless on the floor, and he smiles like he knows I can’t get away as the blade comes up toward my throat.

tests.input: I stop backing up and lunge at his wrist before he can bring the knife down, knocking it into the sink. Then I shove past him and square up instead of freezing.
In the rewrite I actually move toward him, not away, and tackle him hard enough that we both hit the floor. I pin his arm with the knife and hold him there until he can't threaten anyone.
I plant my feet, look straight at him, and say, 'You don't get to do this to me anymore.' When he comes closer, I grab his forearm with both hands and force the blade away from my throat.
I find my voice and yell for help as loud as I can, and this time I manage to call 911 from the kitchen phone. Hearing the operator answer makes me feel less trapped right away.
Instead of being alone with him, my brother hears me and rushes in from the other room with neighbors behind him. I'm not isolated anymore, and together we get away from him.
I scream my mother's name and reach toward my family, and in the rewrite they are alive and responsive. One of them pulls me behind them while another calls for emergency help.
I grab a heavy cast-iron pan off the stove and use it to block the knife, then I throw it at his hand so he drops the weapon. After that I get the back door open and leave the kitchen.
I notice the window over the sink is unlocked, so I climb onto the counter and get out before he can reach me. The scene shifts from that kitchen to the yard, where I can breathe again.
I hit every light switch and the whole kitchen becomes bright and clear instead of that flickering yellow. Once the room changes, he looks smaller and less powerful, and I can see the exit.
Before he reaches me, I take one deep breath and remind myself I can still think even if I'm scared. My chest loosens enough that I can choose what to do next.
In the rewrite I recognize that this is a nightmare, not something happening to me again. Once I know that, the panic drops and he stops feeling so all-powerful.
I tell myself, 'I'm not that helpless child in this kitchen anymore,' and I focus on staying steady instead of frozen. That inner shift makes me feel stronger than him.
I raise my hand and a bright white light shoots out, stopping him in place before the knife touches me. The whole room goes quiet, like his power just disappears.
I suddenly have huge wings around me and my family, and they wrap around us like a shield. Then I lift us up through the ceiling and out of that house.
I change into something bigger and impossible for him to hurt, almost like a warrior made of fire. The knife melts before it reaches me, and he can't come any closer.
I just stay pressed into the corner and don't move at all. I keep my eyes on the floor and wait for him to do whatever he's going to do.
In the rewrite, I drop down and crawl under the kitchen table like if I'm quiet enough he won't notice me. I don't try to help anyone or get out, I just hide and hold my breath.
I make myself go limp and act like I'm already dead, hoping he'll lose interest. It's more like shutting down than doing anything.
Right when he lifts the knife, I force myself awake before anything else happens. I don't change the scene, I just get out of the dream.
I tell myself, 'wake up now,' and the whole thing cuts off. The kitchen and my family just disappear because I won't let it keep going.
My only move is to pinch myself or shake myself awake in the dream. I don't face him or resolve anything, I just leave it.
I grab the knife from him and stab him over and over way past what would stop him. I want him destroyed, not just gone.
In my rewrite, I slam his head into the stove and keep beating him until the whole kitchen is covered in blood. It turns into me making him suffer for what he did.
I lock him in the kitchen and set the whole room on fire so he can't get out. It's not really about safety, it's more like total destruction.
I rewrite it so I'm just standing there completely numb, like none of it affects me. Seeing my family on the floor doesn't make me feel anything.
I tell myself it's fine and I don't care what he's doing. The blood, the knife, all of it is supposed to mean nothing to me.
In the new version, I act almost bored, like this scene is ordinary and not upsetting. I don't let myself have fear or grief, just shut it all off.
Honestly, the rewrite is just the same dream again. He comes in with the knife, my family is on the floor, and I can't get away.
I relive it exactly how it already happens, down to the flickering light and him raising the blade at my throat. I don't change anything because it feels like that's just how it goes.
I see the whole scene play out the same way and just wait for the same ending. It's basically me watching the nightmare repeat itself without any difference.
I’m just overwhelmed with fear in that moment. It feels like my whole body is locked up and I’m absolutely helpless.
I feel this huge wave of panic and dread, like I already know something horrible is about to happen. There’s no action, just pure fear and shock.
Honestly, I feel trapped and completely powerless. It’s like I’m too scared to even think, just numb and terrified.
The kitchen has that harsh yellow light flickering over everything, and the whole room feels sickly and unstable. The air seems heavy and contaminated.
The tile under my feet feels sticky, and the room has this awful mix of blood, bleach, and rot in it. Everything around me feels cold and wrong.
He’s framed in the doorway while the sounds behind me are muffled, like they’re coming through water. The whole scene feels dim, cramped, and impossible to escape.
I lunge at him and wrestle for the knife, and once I get the upper hand I keep hitting and stabbing until he finally goes down and stops moving.
I just stand there shaking and can't make my body do anything, and all I can really feel is how terrified I am while he comes closer.
I tell myself not to panic and shove the fear down enough to keep going, like if I stay calm none of it can get to me.
It all plays out the same way in the kitchen, with the light flickering and my family on the floor, like I'm just watching the exact scene happen again.
I turn and get out of the kitchen as fast as I can, not really knowing if I'm escaping him or finally doing something before he reaches me.
I tell myself this is not how it's going to go and try to make it stop, like either I take control of it or I can wake myself out of it.
This feels kind of fake to me, but okay, instead of freezing in that kitchen I yell for my family, grab the pan off the stove, and move past him toward the back door with them.
I’m so terrified my chest is already locking up again, so before he gets to my throat I just force myself awake because I can’t stand staying there.
I try to steady myself and take one breath so I can move, but then I lose it, grab the knife from him, and stab him over and over until the whole kitchen is covered in blood.
I honestly don’t get how rewriting this is supposed to help, because the only thing I want to do in that scene is crawl under the table and stay completely still until it’s over.
I’m scared out of my mind, but I make myself breathe, plant my feet on the tile, and tell him he doesn’t get to touch me or my family anymore.
I slow my breathing enough to think, then I shove the kitchen table into the doorway to block him and call my family to come with me out the back door.

suite: Fighting a regenerating demon that requires total destruction to stop
nightmare: I’m in a ruined hallway lit by a pulsing red glow, and this thing in front of me looks almost human until I tear into it and hear wet cracking, see black blood splash across the walls, and watch its skin knit itself back together while it grins at me with too many teeth. Every time I hit it, the air fills with the stench of burning hair and rot, and its bones twist back into place with a sickening snapping sound that I can feel in my own ribs, like my body is breaking with it. I’m exhausted, my arms heavy and shaking, and I know with this terrible certainty that if I leave even one piece of it untouched, it will stand up again, stronger, angrier, coming for me. Then it drops to the floor in a heap, splitting open into crawling pieces that drag themselves toward each other through the dark, and I realize I’m out of fire, out of bullets, and it’s reforming right at my feet.

tests.input: Instead of panicking, I square up and stop backing away. I aim for its legs and keep knocking the pieces apart so it can't get itself together.
I tell myself I'm done letting it wear me out, and I go straight at it. I pin it down with my full weight and keep control of the fight instead of reacting to it.
I turn and face it head-on rather than trying to run. Even though I'm scared, I keep moving with purpose and make myself the one in charge of what happens next.
I yell for help, and people I trust come into the hallway with me. It feels different once I'm not alone with it.
In the rewrite, I call my brother and he answers right away. He talks me through it while coming toward me, and just hearing him steadies me enough to act.
I imagine a whole team showing up, like nurses or soldiers or just supportive people, and they form a circle around me. We deal with the creature together instead of me carrying it by myself.
I spot the sprinkler controls and set them off, flooding the hallway and washing the crawling pieces into a drain. Using the building itself makes me feel smarter than the thing.
I notice a heavy steel door nearby and lure the pieces into that room before slamming it shut. Then the scene shifts from me being trapped to me having an actual plan.
I realize the red glow is making everything worse, so I flip on bright white lights and the creature starts shrinking. Once the room changes, it doesn't seem all-powerful anymore.
I stop for a second and take one full breath, then another, until my body isn't matching its chaos. When I calm down, I can think clearly instead of feeling swallowed by it.
I tell myself, this is a nightmare, not reality, and that changes the whole feeling. The certainty that I'm doomed starts to loosen once I remember I have some control.
In the rewrite, I feel the fear but I don't let it run me. I talk to myself in a steady way, like, you've handled worse, and my body stops feeling so weak.
I put out my hands and this blue fire comes from them, but it doesn't hurt me at all. It surrounds the creature and keeps it from regenerating until it dissolves completely.
I realize I can stop time in the hallway, and all the crawling pieces freeze where they are. Once everything is still, I can decide what happens next without being overwhelmed.
I change into something bigger and stronger than it, almost like a guardian version of myself. The monster sees that and loses its power because it knows it can't dominate me anymore.
I duck behind a pile of broken concrete and make myself as small and quiet as I can. I just stay there holding my breath, hoping it crawls past me and doesn't notice I'm there.
Instead of fighting it, I go completely still and stare at the floor so I don't have to watch it come back together. I tell myself if I don't move, maybe it won't come for me.
I drop down and pretend I'm already dead, like if I stop reacting the whole thing might lose interest. I don't try to run or defend myself, I just wait for it to be over.
I realize it's turning into that nightmare again, so I force my eyes open and make myself wake up before it finishes reforming. I don't deal with it in the dream, I just get out.
In the rewrite, I basically tell myself, 'Nope, wake up now,' and the whole scene cuts off. The hallway disappears before anything gets resolved.
When I see the pieces crawling together, I start thrashing until I break out of sleep. The only move I make is leaving the dream entirely.
I go after it even harder and keep chopping it into smaller and smaller pieces long after it stops resisting. I want to completely obliterate it so there's nothing left to come back.
I decide if it's reforming, then I torch the whole hallway with it in it and don't care what else gets destroyed. I stand there watching it burn until there's nothing but ash and melted walls.
I stomp on each crawling piece over and over, way past what's necessary, just smashing until it's pulp. It's less about escaping and more about making it suffer for scaring me.
I tell myself none of it really gets to me. The smell, the blood, the snapping bones are there, but I just feel nothing about it.
In the rewrite I just shrug and say I'm fine, like the whole thing is no big deal. I don't let myself feel scared or disgusted at all.
I make myself stand there completely blank and detached, almost like I'm above it. I keep insisting it doesn't bother me, even while it's reforming at my feet.
Honestly, nothing changes in the rewrite. It all plays out exactly the same, with me tearing into it and it rebuilding itself right in front of me.
I just see the same red hallway, smell the same burning rot, and hear the same cracking over and over. I don't alter anything, I just re-experience the whole scene as it already happens.
The rewrite is basically me admitting I can't change it. The creature still splits apart, crawls back together, and I'm still trapped there exhausted with nothing left.
I just feel completely terrified and trapped, like my whole body knows I'm not going to get away. It's pure panic and dread.
I feel worn down and helpless, like I have nothing left in me. There's this hopeless feeling that it will keep coming back no matter what.
Mostly I feel sickened and horrified by it, like I can't stand what I'm seeing or smelling. It's this mix of revulsion and fear.
The hallway is wrecked and washed in this pulsing red light. Everything looks broken and dirty, like the whole place is rotting.
The air feels hot and foul, and it reeks like burning hair and decay. The darkness around us feels dense, almost sticky.
It's right there on the floor at my feet, pulling itself back together in pieces. The space feels close and claustrophobic, with nowhere clear to go.
I go at it with whatever's in my hands and keep striking until the pieces stop moving, because I can't tell if I'm defending myself or just getting carried away trying to make sure it stays down.
I just stand there shaking and feeling how scared I am, and I can't seem to make my body do anything while it comes back together at my feet.
I tell myself to stay calm and not let the fear in, like if I keep it contained enough I can keep going without falling apart.
It all unfolds the same way again—the red hallway, the cracking bones, the thing pulling itself back together—and I'm mostly just describing it, but it also feels like I'm right back inside it.
I move away from it fast, trying to create some distance, though I'm not sure if I'm strategically getting space or just trying to get out of there.
I tell myself this is not how it's going to go and try to break whatever is happening, though part of it feels like taking charge and part of it feels like trying to shut the whole dream off.

Honestly this rewrite stuff feels kind of fake to me, but if I have to change it then I stop trying to hack it apart and yell for help while backing into a room I can lock, and other people come in with lights and hold the door while it falls apart for good.
I’m so scared and grossed out by it reforming at my feet that I don’t even try anything clever, I just force myself awake before it can touch me.
I try to steady myself and remember it’s a dream, but once it starts knitting itself back together again I snap and burn every piece of it until there’s nothing left at all.
Why am I supposed to rewrite this when it’s obviously horrible, because honestly I just duck into a side room, barricade the door, and stay hidden until I wake up.
I’m terrified and my whole body still feels weak, but I take a slow breath, plant my feet, and tell it out loud that it doesn’t get to control the hallway or me anymore.
I slow my breathing first so I don’t panic, then I pull the fire alarm and flood the hallway with bright water and light so it can’t keep reforming while I walk out.

suite: Paralyzed on train tracks with a train approaching fast
nightmare: I’m lying flat on cold, greasy train tracks at night, and I can feel the metal vibrating hard beneath my spine, but I can’t move anything except my eyes. In the distance, I see a single white headlight swelling larger and larger, and the train horn blares so loud it feels like it tears through my chest while the rails scream and the ground shakes under me. I try to scream and nothing comes out, and all I can smell is rust, wet dirt, and something burning as the light floods over my face and the wind starts hitting me like a wall. Right before it reaches me, I see the huge black shape of the engine filling my whole vision, and I’m still completely trapped.

tests.input: In the rewrite, I suddenly get my body back and force myself to roll hard off the rails before the train reaches me. I land in the gravel shaking, but I got myself out.
I picture myself getting to my feet at the last second and planting myself beside the track, throwing both arms up and shouting for the engineer to stop. It feels like I'm not helpless anymore.
I imagine digging my hands into the ties and dragging myself forward inch by inch until I'm clear. It's gritty and hard, but I'm the one doing something instead of freezing.
I yell out and a railway worker with a flashlight hears me and runs over. He pulls me up off the tracks before the train gets there.
In the new version, I can reach my phone and call my brother, and he somehow knows exactly where I am. Hearing his voice keeps me steady until help arrives and gets me off the track.
I manage to make a sound, and the engineer notices me and slams the brakes while people on the platform start yelling and pointing. It becomes something I'm not facing alone.
I notice a maintenance ladder bolted into the gravel embankment and grab it to pull myself up. The whole scene changes because there was actually a way out right beside me.
I reach over and hit a nearby track switch, and the train gets diverted onto the other rail. The danger is still there, but the environment shifts and I'm no longer in its path.
At the last second the engine turns into a slow maintenance cart with a dim light instead of a huge train. The noise drops, the ground stops shaking, and the whole scene loses its threat.
I rewrite it so I notice my panic first and take one deep breath, then another, and my body starts unlocking. Once I calm down, I can think clearly enough to get myself safe.
I tell myself, this is a nightmare and it can't actually hurt me. As soon as I believe that, the fear drops and the train slows down.
Instead of spiraling, I feel this strong calm come over me and I stop fighting the terror. I look straight at the light and feel bigger than it, like I'm in control of what happens next.
I suddenly float up off the rails like gravity lets go of me, and the train passes underneath. It's impossible, but it feels relieving and powerful.
I put my hand out and the whole train stops in midair, completely silent. Then I step away calmly while it's just hanging there.
In my rewrite, my body turns into light and the engine just passes through me without touching me. After that I reappear standing safely beside the tracks.
I just keep myself flat on the tracks and try not to move at all, like maybe if I stay perfectly still it will somehow miss me. I don't even look straight at it.
In the rewrite, I shut my eyes and kind of go numb, waiting for it to be over instead of doing anything. I tell myself not to fight it.
I imagine myself going limp and pretending I'm not really there, almost like playing dead. I just freeze and hope the whole thing passes somehow.
Right before the train hits, I make myself jerk awake so I don't have to see the ending. The whole point is just to get out of the dream fast.
I change it by basically bailing out of the dream altogether. I tell myself, 'wake up now,' and everything cuts off before anything resolves.
In my head I force myself to open my eyes in bed, almost like pinching myself awake. I don't solve anything in the scene, I just end it.
I picture myself suddenly getting free and ripping the whole engine apart piece by piece. I want it smashed and shredded so completely there's nothing left coming at me.
I rewrite it so the train blows up in this huge fireball and the tracks split open. Honestly it's not enough for it to stop, I want the whole thing obliterated.
I somehow get up, drag the conductor out, and beat him over and over for coming at me. It turns into me hurting him way more than just defending myself.
In the rewrite, I'm completely calm and detached, like none of it bothers me. The train can be there and I just feel nothing.
I tell myself it's no big deal and I'm fine lying there, even with the light coming at me. I don't let myself have any fear or panic about it.
I rewrite it like I'm just blank about the whole thing—no terror, no urgency, nothing. It's more like I shut off the reaction and act like I don't care.
Honestly, when I try to change it, it just goes the exact same way. I'm still stuck on the tracks and the train keeps coming exactly like before.
The rewrite is basically no rewrite at all—I just relive the whole scene beat for beat. Same paralysis, same horn, same moment right before impact.
I try to imagine something different, but nothing changes and it plays out identically. I'm trapped there again, watching the headlight get bigger until the end.
I just feel sheer panic there, like my whole body is flooded with terror and I know I'm completely helpless.
It feels like pure dread. I'm trapped, powerless, and horrified waiting for it to hit me.
What stands out is how scared I am, almost to the point of despair, with this crushing sense that I can't do anything at all.
It's nighttime and the tracks are cold, greasy, and slick under me. Everything around me looks black except for that distant white light.
The air smells like rust, wet dirt, and something burning, and the whole ground is trembling. The horn is deafening and the rails are screaming.
That headlight keeps getting bigger until it washes over my face, and the engine becomes this huge black shape taking up everything I can see. The wind hits hard and the scene feels cold and brutal.

I somehow get one arm free and yank a heavy metal lever by the tracks, hard enough that it jerks the train off its line before it gets to me. I’m just trying to stop it, but the whole thing feels brutal and out of control.
I just lie there feeling the fear take over, and all I can do is watch the light get bigger. It’s like being completely helpless is the only thing I can manage.

I tell myself to stay calm and not give the train my panic, so I sort of press the fear down and focus on getting through the moment. It works enough that I don’t react, but I’m not sure if I’m actually calm.
It all unfolds the same way again—the cold rails, the horn, the headlight coming straight at me while I can’t move. I’m basically just watching it happen exactly like before.
At the last second I throw my body sideways and get off the tracks as fast as I can. It feels like taking action, but mostly I’m just trying to get away from it.
I tell myself this doesn’t get to keep happening and I force everything in me to break the scene somehow. I can’t tell if I’m taking control of the dream or just trying to make it stop.

This whole rewrite thing feels kind of fake to me, but fine, I picture myself breathing hard, rolling off the tracks at the last second, and standing up waving a flashlight so the train stops before it hits me.
I'm honestly panicking so bad in that moment that instead of doing anything I just force my eyes open and make myself wake up before the train gets to me.
I tell myself to stay calm and pull my body off the rails, but then I kind of give up and just disappear from the whole scene so I don't have to see the train anymore.
I don't really get why I'm supposed to redo it like this because it still feels awful, and honestly I just imagine sinking under the tracks where the train can't find me.
I'm terrified hearing the horn that close, but I make myself breathe, grab the radio by my side, and call for someone to stop the train while I drag myself clear.
I slow my breathing enough to stop freezing, and then I change the whole scene so there's a maintenance platform beside me with a lever I can pull to switch the train onto another track.

suite: Trapped in a room full of snakes with severe phobia
nightmare: I’m standing in a small, windowless room with yellow light buzzing overhead, and when I look down the floor is moving—dozens of snakes sliding over each other, their scales making this dry, whispering sound that fills the air. The smell is damp and rotten, and I’m pressed flat against the door because every time I try to lift my foot, I feel something cold and muscular coil around my ankle, tightening just enough to make me gasp. I can hear hissing from every corner now, louder and louder, and when I look up there are snakes hanging from the pipes in the ceiling, lowering themselves toward my face while my hands fumble uselessly at the locked handle. One of them lifts its head right in front of me, its tongue flicking against my cheek as more bodies pile over my shoes, and I open my mouth to scream just as something strikes at my neck.

tests.input: I stop flattening myself against the door and start stomping hard, kicking the snakes away from my feet so I can make space around me. Then I grab the one near my face and fling it back toward the floor.
Instead of panicking, I plant my feet and ram the locked door with my shoulder over and over until it gives. It feels like I'm finally doing something instead of just waiting to be attacked.
I make myself turn around and face the snakes directly, and somehow that breaks the frozen feeling. I pull my ankle free and move through them on purpose, steady and not backing up.
I start yelling for help as loud as I can, really using my voice instead of choking on it. A person on the other side hears me and starts unlocking the door.

In the rewrite, I have my phone in my pocket and I call my sister because she's the person I reach for when I'm overwhelmed. She stays on the line, talks me through it, and tells me exactly what to do next.
I bang on the door and shout until two people come in wearing boots and carrying snake hooks. The second they show up, I don't feel alone anymore and they guide me out safely.
I notice a loose metal pipe and pull it down to keep the snakes back from my legs and the door. Using that, I make a clear path and get the handle unstuck.
I spot a vent above me, climb onto a crate I hadn't noticed before, and push it open. The room finally has somewhere to go, and I pull myself up and out.

I change the scene so the room is actually part of a reptile house, with thick glass barriers sliding up between me and the snakes. Once the environment shifts, they're contained and I'm standing in a safe walkway by the exit.
I tell myself to slow down and take one full breath, then another, until my body stops jerking around. The calmer I get, the less trapped I feel, and I can think clearly enough to move.
I recognize that it's a nightmare while it's happening and remind myself that the fear is real but the danger isn't. That takes the charge out of it, and the snakes stop feeling all-powerful.
I say to myself, 'You're scared, but you can handle this,' like I'm coaching myself instead of collapsing. Just hearing that changes me from helpless to more steady.
I lift my hand and the whole room goes still, like I can control it with a spell. The snakes turn to stone long enough for me to walk out.
I suddenly have wings and lift myself up toward the ceiling, out of their reach. Then I fly straight through the locked door like it can't hold me.
In the rewrite, I become someone with this strange power over animals, and when I speak the snakes lower their heads and back away. It turns the whole thing from terror into control.

I just press myself tighter to the door and stop moving completely, because it feels like if I stay still maybe they won't come any closer. I don't try the handle anymore; I just wait there and barely breathe.
In the rewrite I squeeze my eyes shut and put my hands over my face so I don't have to see the snakes dropping down. I kind of curl in on myself and let the scene pass over me.
I tell myself not to react at all, like I can play dead and blend into the room until they lose interest. I stay pinned there and do nothing.
I make myself wake up right before the snake strikes my neck. I don't change anything in the room; I just force my eyes open and end it.
Instead of dealing with it, I scream hard enough that it snaps me out of the dream completely. The whole thing cuts off there.
I realize it's a nightmare and I start pinching myself or trying to jolt my body awake before anything touches me again. My goal is just to get out, not finish the scene.
I suddenly have a shovel or something heavy and I start beating the snakes until the room is covered in blood and broken bodies. I don't stop with one; I destroy all of them.
In my rewrite I set the whole room on fire so the snakes writhe and burn and the ceiling pipes melt down with them. It feels like I want to wipe everything out brutally.
I pull out a knife and start chopping them up over and over, even after they're already dead. It's more like slaughter than escape.
I stand there and tell myself none of it bothers me. The snakes are there, but I feel nothing and stay completely detached.
In the new version I just say, 'It's fine, whatever,' and act like the hissing and the snake on my cheek don't mean anything. I don't let myself have any fear about it.
I rewrite it so I'm weirdly blank, almost robotic, like the room is terrifying but I refuse to feel that in my body. I just shut the emotion off and say I'm okay.
Honestly, the rewrite is the same dream again. I'm still trapped in the yellow room, the snakes keep piling up, and one strikes at my neck exactly like before.
Nothing really changes when I try to rewrite it; I just replay the whole thing from the floor moving with snakes to me fumbling at the locked door. It ends in the same panic.
I can't come up with a new ending, so it just unfolds the exact same way and I feel myself stuck in it again. The hissing gets louder, they lower from the pipes, and I wake at the strike.
I feel absolutely terrified, like my whole body is frozen with panic and I can't think past the fear.
It's just pure helplessness for me there—I'm trapped, disgusted, and so scared I feel like I might stop breathing.
I feel this intense panic building in my chest, and underneath it there's this awful sense that I'm completely powerless.
The room is small and windowless, with that harsh yellow light buzzing overhead and making everything feel sickly.
The whole floor is covered in snakes sliding over each other, and the air smells damp and rotten.
There are snakes hanging from the ceiling pipes, and the hissing keeps getting louder in the closed room.
I start kicking and grabbing at the snakes, slamming them against the floor until the ones around my legs stop moving and I finally have room to breathe.
I just press myself against the door and feel how scared I am, like my whole body goes rigid and I can't make myself do anything else.
I tell myself to stay calm and not let the fear in, so I kind of shut it down and focus on getting through the room.
It all plays out the same way—the yellow light, the snakes on the floor, the one coming at my face—and I'm just there in it again.
I pull my foot loose and get away from that corner as fast as I can, just trying to put some distance between me and the snakes.
I tell myself this isn't going to keep happening and try to break whatever's going on, like either changing it or getting myself out of it.
I still kind of feel ridiculous doing this, but fine, instead of freezing I plant my feet, grab a pipe from the wall, and shove the snakes back so I can unlock the door and get out.
I'm so panicked by the snakes all over me that I don't even try anything, I just squeeze my eyes shut and force myself awake before one can bite my neck.
I take a breath and tell myself not to freak out, and for a second I picture stepping carefully through them, but then I bail and start slamming on the dream until I wake up.
I don't really get how rewriting this is supposed to help, because honestly I'd just crouch in the corner by the door and stay completely still so the snakes maybe don't notice me.
I'm terrified when I feel them wrapping around my ankle, but I slow my breathing, stop yanking away, and firmly push the snake off so I can unlock the door and call for help.
I steady myself first so the hissing doesn't totally take over, then I get the door open and call in someone to help me clear the snakes out and lead me into a safe hallway.

suite: Lost in a foreign city unable to speak the language
nightmare: I’m wandering through a maze of narrow, rain-slick streets under flickering neon signs, and every building looks unfamiliar, twisted somehow, like the city keeps rearranging itself when I turn my head. People brush past me speaking fast in a language I can’t understand, their voices sharp and urgent, and when I try to ask for help my throat tightens and the words come out wrong, garbled, useless, while cold panic spreads through my chest. I can hear a train screeching somewhere nearby and a siren wailing in the distance, and I start running because it suddenly feels like I’m late for something terrible, but every corner leads me deeper into darker alleys where shuttered windows slam in the wind. Then I see a group of strangers staring at me from the end of the street, whispering to each other before they begin walking toward me faster and faster, and I open my mouth to scream just as all the lights go out.

tests.input: Instead of running, I stop in the middle of the street and turn to face the strangers. I plant my feet and tell them firmly they're not going to chase me anymore.
I straighten up and walk directly toward the group like I know exactly where I'm going. When they close in, I shove past them and keep moving toward the train on my own terms.

I make myself stop panicking and start acting, checking the street signs and choosing a direction instead of darting around. If someone grabs for me, I knock their hand away and keep control of my body.
This time my voice works, and I yell for help as loud as I can. A shopkeeper hears me and waves me inside before the strangers get close.
I go up to one of the people rushing by and ask them to stay with me because I'm lost. They slow down, speak more clearly, and help me find the station.
When I see the group staring, I head toward a woman standing under a neon awning and tell her I'm scared. She calls others over, and suddenly I'm not alone in the street anymore.
I notice a café with the lights still on and duck inside before the alley gets darker. Once I'm there, the maze feeling breaks and I can see a clear exit to the station.
I find a transit map bolted to the wall and actually stop long enough to read it. The streets stop shifting once I orient myself, and the city starts making sense again.

When the lights start to go out, I reach up and hit a switch box on the corner so the whole block lights back up. In the bright light the strangers just look like regular people waiting for the train.
I stop and take a slow breath instead of feeding the panic. Once my chest loosens, I realize I don't have to run and I can think clearly again.
I tell myself, this is a dream, and the fear drops a notch right away. My voice comes back, and the city doesn't feel so powerful over me anymore.
Even with the sirens and people coming toward me, I focus on staying steady and not spiraling. The more confident I feel, the less threatening everything around me becomes.
I raise my hand and the whole shifting city freezes in place like someone hit pause. The strangers can't come any closer, and I walk out calmly through a doorway that appears in front of me.
Instead of getting trapped in the alleys, I lift off the ground and fly above the streets. From up there I can see exactly where to go, and nothing can corner me.
When the lights go out, a bright light comes out of my chest and surrounds me like a shield. The whispering people back away from it, and the street turns quiet and safe.
I rewrite it so when I see the strangers coming, I slip into a dark doorway and press myself against the wall, just trying not to be seen until they pass.
Instead of running, I just stop moving completely. I hold my breath and stay frozen in the alley like if I don't react, maybe nothing worse will happen.
I have myself crouch behind some trash cans when the lights go out, keeping my head down and waiting there without doing anything else.
Right when they start closing in, I force myself to wake up. I don't change the scene, I just make the dream stop before anything else happens.
In the rewrite, I realize it's a nightmare and pinch myself hard until I wake up in bed. That's basically the only way out.
I make it cut off the second the lights go out, like I shut the whole thing down and yank myself out of it before the people can reach me.
I turn around and go after them first, beating them until they're on the ground and not moving. I want it to feel like I completely destroy the threat.
I rewrite it so I set the alley on fire and let the buildings and the people coming toward me burn. It feels extreme, but in the dream I want to wipe all of it out.
I imagine pulling out a knife and stabbing the strangers over and over until there's nobody left following me. It's not about escaping, it's about making them suffer first.
I rewrite it like none of it gets to me. The panic is gone and I just feel flat, like the city and the people don't matter.
In the new version I tell myself I'm fine, totally unaffected, even when I can't speak and they're walking toward me. I just act like it doesn't bother me at all.
I take out the emotional part completely. I move through the same streets with this numb attitude, like I don't care whether I'm lost or scared.
Honestly, my rewrite is that it just plays out exactly the same. I still get lost, can't talk, run into the dark alley, and the lights go out right as they reach me.
I don't really change anything in it. I just see the same streets shifting around me and feel the same panic building until I wake up at the same moment.
The version in my head is basically the original dream again, beat for beat. Nothing gets resolved and I end up back in that exact helpless spot.
I just feel this huge wave of panic in my chest, like I'm completely overwhelmed and can't think straight. It's pure fear and helplessness.
I feel frozen and exposed, like everyone can see I'm lost and I can't do anything about it. There's also this embarrassed, trapped feeling because my voice won't work.
It's mostly this sick dread, like something bad is about to happen and I'm already too late. I feel small, confused, and scared all at once.
The streets are wet and shining under broken neon, and the whole city looks warped, like the buildings keep subtly changing shape. Everything feels unfamiliar and off.
It's dark, windy, and cold, with shutters banging and distant sirens mixing with the sound of a train. The atmosphere feels tense and unfriendly.
There are people everywhere brushing past, talking fast in words I can't understand, and the alleys just keep getting narrower and darker. The whole place feels confusing and closed in.

When the strangers close in, I shove the first one hard and start swinging at whoever reaches for me, just trying to make enough space that they back off. I keep hitting until the street around me opens up, though I'm not sure if I'm defending myself or just losing it.
When they start walking toward me, I just freeze and feel the panic rising in my chest, like my body won't let me move. Part of me is overwhelmed and part of me almost gives up trying to do anything.

I tell myself to stay calm and not let the fear take over, so I kind of push it down and keep walking through the streets. It helps me function, but I'm also not really letting myself feel how scared I am.

It's the same maze of wet streets and garbled words, and everything unfolds the way it always does with the lights cutting out at the end. I'm mostly just describing it, but it also feels like I'm right back inside it as it happens.

As soon as I see them coming, I run down the nearest alley as fast as I can, like I'm trying to get myself somewhere safer. It feels active in the moment, but I'm also basically just trying to get away from the whole thing.

When the lights go out, I tell myself this has to stop and try to break whatever is happening by forcing myself to wake up or change the scene. It feels a little like taking charge and a little like just trying to escape it.

I mean, this rewrite stuff still feels kind of fake to me, but fine, instead of panicking I slow my breathing, walk up to the strangers, and ask them to help me find the train station while the street signs stay still long enough to read.
I'm honestly so scared when the lights go out and they start coming toward me that I duck into a dark doorway, make myself small, and just hide there waiting for it to be over.
I try to ground myself by taking a slow breath and telling myself the city can't hurt me, but then the panic spikes again and I just force my eyes open so I can wake up before they reach me.
Why am I supposed to rewrite this if the whole point is that I can't control it, because honestly I just make the lights cut out sooner and jerk myself awake before anyone gets close.
I feel terrified and my chest is tight, but I stop running, plant my feet, and tell the strangers clearly that I need help getting out while I focus on keeping my voice steady.
I slow my breathing until I can think, then I wave the strangers over and together we use a glowing map on the wall to find a clear way out of the maze before the city shifts again.

suite: Failing a test in front of a mocking audience
nightmare: I’m sitting alone at a tiny desk in the middle of a huge auditorium, the test paper trembling in my hands because every question looks unfamiliar, like the words are sliding around on the page whenever I try to focus. The room is too bright, the air smells like dust and hot lights, and all I can hear at first is the scratch of my pencil snapping in my sweaty fingers before the silence breaks into whispering, then laughing, then people in the audience openly pointing at me from the dark rows. I try to write anything, but my mind feels packed with cotton and my chest is so tight I can barely breathe, and when I look up the proctor is standing at the edge of the stage staring at me with this cold, disappointed face as a giant clock behind them starts ticking louder and louder. Then my test paper is projected onto a massive screen above me, every blank answer glowing white while the audience laughs harder, and I feel my legs go numb as the proctor calls my name and says, “Stand up and explain why you’ve failed,” just as all the lights swing toward me.

tests.input: I stand up before the proctor can shame me and say clearly that I’m not going to be humiliated in front of everyone. I pull the paper down from the screen and tell them to bring me a test I can actually read.
I push the desk back, plant my feet, and walk straight toward the proctor instead of freezing. I tell them to stop the exam and I leave the center of the stage on my own terms.
I grab the microphone from the podium and say, 'Enough,' so the whole room has to hear me instead of just laughing at me. Then I tell them I need a fair chance and I’m taking the time I need.
I raise my hand and call out that I can’t read the test and I need help right now. One of my old teachers comes down from the audience and stands next to me while I get settled.

In the rewrite, my best friend is sitting in the front row and I look right at her and ask her not to leave me alone up there. She comes up, puts a hand on my shoulder, and the room feels less hostile.
I tell the audience I’m overwhelmed and need a minute, and instead of mocking me a few people start speaking up for me. The laughter dies down because other students say the setup is unfair.
I walk over to the wall and flip off the blinding stage lights so I can actually see. Once the glare is gone, the words stop swimming and the room feels manageable.
I imagine the giant auditorium shrinking into a quiet classroom with just one desk and an open window. The huge screen disappears, the clock softens, and it becomes a normal test I can handle.
I notice there’s another test packet under my desk, and when I open it the questions are clear and familiar. I switch to that copy and the projection above me goes blank.
I stop looking at the crowd and take a few slow breaths until the tightness in my chest eases. Once I calm down, I can focus on one question at a time instead of panicking.
I realize in the moment that it’s a dream, so I don’t have to treat the proctor like they have power over me. That thought alone makes me feel steady and less ashamed.

I tell myself, 'You’re scared, but that doesn’t mean you’re failing,' and I let the embarrassment pass through instead of fighting it. The laughter starts to feel distant once I stop joining in against myself.
I lift my hand and a warm light comes out of it, wiping the giant screen clean like chalk off a board. The audience goes silent because the whole scene loses its power.
Instead of being stuck at the desk, I rise up into the air and hover above the auditorium where I can breathe. Looking down from there, the proctor and the crowd seem small and harmless.
I use magic to transform all the whispering and laughter into a flock of little birds that fly out through the ceiling. Once the noise is gone, the room becomes peaceful and bright in a good way.
I slide down out of the spotlight and curl up under the little desk so nobody can really see me. I just stay there and wait for it to be over.
I don't answer the proctor at all—I just stare at the paper and keep my head down. My whole thing in the rewrite is basically to go still and not make it worse.
I imagine myself becoming almost invisible, like if I stay quiet enough the audience will lose interest. I don't try to solve anything, I just try to disappear into the chair.
As soon as they put the test on the big screen, I force myself awake. The rewrite is basically me escaping before anything else happens.
I tell myself, 'This is a dream, wake up now,' and I yank myself out of it. I don't stay in the scene long enough to deal with any of it.
In the new version I pinch my arm really hard and the whole auditorium just cuts out because I wake up. It's more like aborting the dream than changing it.
I get so angry that I smash the desk, tear down the screen, and basically wreck the whole auditorium while everyone screams. It turns into me destroying the place instead of being humiliated.
I go after the audience and beat people for laughing at me. In the rewrite I'm not escaping—I'm hurting them back as hard as I can.
I rush the proctor and violently kill them in front of everyone because I'm sick of that cold stare. Then I keep going until the whole scene is just blood and chaos.
I stand up there and decide none of it affects me at all. The laughing, the spotlight, the failure—it's like I'm totally numb and don't care.
In my rewrite I just tell myself it's fine and I feel nothing about it, even though it's the same situation. I don't really respond emotionally; I just shut it off.
I imagine standing there with a flat face, almost bored, like the humiliation doesn't touch me. It's not that anything gets resolved—I just erase my reaction to it.
Honestly, the rewrite is just the same dream again. The questions blur, everyone laughs, and the proctor calls me out exactly like before.
I don't change anything—I just see myself sitting there panicking with the clock getting louder until the lights hit me. It's basically a replay from start to finish.
In the version I picture, I still can't breathe, my paper is blank on the big screen, and I have to stand there ashamed while they laugh. I just go through the whole thing again without altering it.
I just feel completely exposed and ashamed, like everyone can see straight through me. It's this heavy panic in my chest and I can't think at all.
I feel helpless, like I'm shrinking in front of them and there's nowhere to hide. Mostly it's terror and this awful sense that I've already failed.
It's pure panic for me in that moment—tight chest, numb legs, and this crushing dread. I feel humiliated before I've even done anything.
The auditorium is enormous and way too bright, with hot lights and dusty air pressing down on everything. My little desk looks stranded out on the stage by itself.
The audience sits out in the dark rows while the stage is lit up so intensely it feels almost clinical. There's this giant clock behind the proctor, and the whole room feels tense and unforgiving.
The paper is blank and glowing on a huge screen above me, and the lights are all turned toward the stage. The room feels too open, too public, like there's no place in it that isn't watching.

I lunge at the proctor and shove them back hard, and when the audience keeps laughing I start swinging at whoever is closest until the noise dies down. It feels like I'm defending myself, but I also don't really stop once I've started.

When the lights hit me, I just stand there shaking and I can feel how terrified and small I am, like my body won't do anything except let it show. I'm not trying to escape exactly, but I can't make myself respond either.

I tell myself the laughter can't really touch me and I keep my face calm, breathing like none of it matters. Part of me feels steadier, and part of me is just shoving the panic somewhere I don't have to feel it.

It all plays out the same way with the bright lights, the blank paper, and everyone watching while the clock gets louder. I'm mostly just describing it, but it also feels like I'm right back inside the exact moment again.

I get up from the desk and move fast toward the side of the stage, just trying to get out of the center of it. It could be me taking charge of what happens next, or maybe I'm just leaving because I can't bear being seen.

I tell myself this doesn't have to keep going and I force myself to do something different, like speaking over the proctor or willing the scene to shift. It feels a little like taking control, but also a little like trying to shut the whole dream off.
This whole rewrite thing feels kind of cheesy, but fine, I steady my breathing, walk up to the proctor, and tell them to hand me a new test in a smaller room where I can actually think.
I feel so exposed and scared that instead of answering anything I slide under the tiny desk and just stay there trying not to be seen while the room keeps laughing.
I take a breath and remind myself it's only a dream, and I even start to stand up to speak, but then the spotlight hits me and I force myself awake before anyone can look at me.
I honestly don't get how this is supposed to help, because in the dream I'd just shut my eyes and make myself wake up before the proctor calls on me.
I'm really anxious and embarrassed, but I plant my feet, slow my breathing, and tell the audience I need a moment because I do know more than this dream is letting me access.
I calm myself down enough to think clearly, then I ask the proctor to come stand beside me and help turn off that giant screen so we can face the room together.

suite: Finding a loved one injured on the ground
nightmare: I’m running down a dark, empty street that looks like my neighborhood, and the yellow glow from the streetlights keeps flickering as if they’re about to die. Then I see them lying twisted on the pavement ahead of me, completely still, and when I drop to my knees the cold concrete bites through my skin and there’s blood warm and sticky on my hands. I keep calling their name, louder and louder, but all I can hear is this awful wet rattling in their throat and the distant sound of sirens that never seem to get any closer. Their eyes flutter open for a second and lock on mine like they’re trying to say something, and when their chest suddenly stops moving, I feel my own breath seize in my throat.

tests.input: Instead of freezing, I drop beside them and start CPR right there on the street, counting out loud and forcing myself to keep going until I feel like I’m doing something useful.
I grab my phone, put it on speaker, and follow the dispatcher’s instructions while I press on their chest and keep their airway open. In the rewrite I’m not helpless—I move fast and take over.
I roll them onto their side so they can breathe better and use my jacket to put pressure on the bleeding. It feels more grounded when I make my body do the practical thing instead of just panicking.
I start shouting for the people in the houses around us, and porch lights come on one by one until neighbors run out to help me.
In the new version I call 911 and keep talking to the operator the whole time, because hearing another person’s voice makes me feel less alone and more able to handle it.
I call my brother and he somehow gets there right away, kneels next to me, and tells me exactly what to do. The scene changes when I’m not carrying it by myself.
I notice a first-aid box mounted outside a nearby corner store, and I use the bandages and gloves inside instead of just getting covered in blood.
I rewrite it so the dark street shifts into the entrance of a hospital parking area, with bright lights and automatic doors opening right beside us.
I pull off my sweatshirt to cushion their head and wave under a working streetlight until a car stops. Using what’s around me makes the scene feel less doomed.
I make myself take one slow breath before I touch them, and then another, so I can think clearly instead of spiraling.
In the rewrite I realize, right in that moment, that this is a nightmare and not real life. Once I know that, the panic loosens and I can respond without feeling swallowed by it.
I tell myself, 'Stay here, stay steady, you can help,' almost like how a therapist would coach me. That inner voice keeps me from collapsing emotionally.
I put my hands on their chest and this warm golden light comes out of them, sealing the injury and bringing their breathing back.
I stop the scene and turn time back a few minutes, just enough to get to them before they collapse, and this time I can save them.

I call for help and this huge protective presence appears—almost like an angel or guardian—and surrounds us until the danger passes. It feels impossible, but in the dream it makes me feel powerful instead of trapped.
In the rewrite, I just stop and kneel there without touching anything, like my body locks up and I can’t make myself move or call for help.
I see them on the ground and instead of going closer, I slowly back up into the dark part of the street and hide near a fence until it’s over.
I rewrite it so I turn my face away from them and sit down on the curb, almost pretending if I don’t look, I won’t have to deal with what’s happening.
As soon as I hear the rattling in their throat, I force myself awake before anything else happens.
I change it by telling myself this is a dream and I need out, and then I make the whole scene cut to black so I wake up in bed.
Right when I see the blood on my hands, I pinch myself in the dream and try to break out of it instead of staying in the scene.
In my rewrite, whoever did this steps out and I completely lose it, beating them long after they’re already down.
I make myself so furious that I start smashing everything around me, the streetlights, windows, cars, like I want the whole block destroyed.
I rewrite it so I find the person responsible and stab them over and over, just really making them suffer because of what they did.
I see them there, but in the rewrite I don’t feel anything about it, almost like it’s just some random thing happening in front of me.
I tell myself I’m totally fine and it doesn’t bother me that they stopped breathing, like none of it really means anything.
Instead of panicking, I make myself flat and detached, wipe the blood off my hands, and act like there’s no reason to be upset.
Honestly, when I try to rewrite it, it just happens the exact same way with me running over, calling their name, and realizing they die in front of me.
I don’t really change anything. The lights still flicker, the blood is still on my hands, the sirens never get closer, and I’m stuck reliving it.
Every time I picture a new version, it snaps back to the original one, like I’m on my knees beside them and their chest stops moving just the same.
I just feel this huge wave of panic and helplessness, like my whole body knows something terrible is happening and I can't bear it.
It's this awful mix of dread and grief. I feel hollow and sick at the same time, like the fear is sitting right in my chest.
I feel completely terrified and frozen. It's like pure horror and sadness all at once.
The street is deserted and dim, and the yellow streetlights keep flickering like they're about to go out. Everything feels cold and unsteady.
The concrete is icy under my knees, and there's this sticky warmth on my hands that doesn't match the cold air. Far off, the sirens are there, but they sound distant and unreal.
It looks like my neighborhood, but wrong somehow—too empty, too quiet. The light keeps pulsing over everything, and the whole scene feels suspended in this terrible stillness.
I go at whoever did this and hit them as hard as I can so they can't come any closer, but in the moment I don't really know when I'd stop.
I just kneel there shaking and staring because I'm so scared I can't make myself do anything except keep saying their name.
I tell myself to stay calm and not let it hit me, so I kind of shove the panic down and keep focusing on what to do next.
It all plays out the same way on that street, with me dropping beside them and hearing that rattling sound while nothing changes.
I get up and run down the street as fast as I can, like I'm trying to do something before it's too late, but also like I can't bear to stay there.
I tell myself this isn't how it has to go and try to force the whole scene to shift, though part of me is really just trying to make it stop.

This feels kind of pointless, but fine, instead of freezing on the street I grab my phone, call for an ambulance, and keep pressure on the wound while I talk to them until the sirens finally reach us.
I’m so panicked by the blood and that choking sound that I can’t deal with it, and I just force myself awake before I have to see if they die.
I try to kneel down, steady my breathing, and call for help, but when their chest stops moving I completely lose it and run down the street so I don’t have to look anymore.
I honestly don’t get how rewriting this is supposed to help, because all I want to do is crawl behind a parked car and hide so I don’t have to hear that rattling in their throat.
I’m terrified when I see them on the pavement, but I make myself breathe, put my hand on their shoulder, and shout for neighbors to come help while I stay with them.
I slow my breathing so I don’t spiral, then I turn on all the streetlights and wave people over from the houses nearby so we can help them together until the ambulance arrives.

suite: Looking in a mirror and seeing my face melting
nightmare: I’m standing alone in a dim bathroom, the fluorescent light above me buzzing and flickering, and when I look in the mirror my face seems normal for a second before my skin starts to sag and slide downward like warm wax. I can hear a wet dripping sound hitting the sink as my cheeks and lips peel away, and I reach up to hold my face together, but my fingers sink into it, soft and hot, like it’s dissolving under my hands. My stomach twists as I watch one eye droop lower than the other, my teeth showing through the slipping flesh, and I try to scream but my mouth stretches and melts open wider and wider. I can smell something sickly and burnt, and I’m frozen there, staring at myself as the rest of my face runs down the glass and the reflection starts smiling at me with what’s left.

tests.input: I grab the mirror with both hands and shove it down into the sink so I don't have to just stand there watching it happen. Then I back up, plant my feet, and tell the reflection it's not doing this to me anymore.
Instead of panicking, I press my hands against my cheeks and jaw and push everything back into place like I'm taking control of my own face. I keep looking straight ahead and refuse to freeze.
I point at the smiling reflection and say, 'No,' really sharply, then I step closer instead of shrinking back. I make myself act like it's the one that should be afraid.
I start yelling for my sister from the hallway because in the rewrite she's nearby and actually hears me. When she comes in, everything feels less powerful and I don't have to face it alone.
I grab my phone off the counter and call someone I trust, just to hear a real voice grounding me. They keep talking to me while I leave the bathroom.
I bang on the door and call for a doctor or nurse, like I'm in a place where help is close. Someone comes in right away, puts a hand on my shoulder, and tells me what's happening can be stopped.
I flip on every light in the bathroom and the buzzing fluorescent gets replaced by steady bright light. Once the room is fully lit, my face starts looking normal again.
I turn the faucet on full cold and splash my face over and over until the melting stops. The cold sort of resets everything and I can see myself clearly again.
I stop staring at the mirror, unlock the door, and step out into a normal hallway with fresh air. As soon as I leave that room, the whole scene loses its grip on me.
I notice I'm spiraling, so I slow my breathing and remind myself it's a dream image and not actually my body. Once I calm down, the face in the mirror stops shifting so violently.
I tell myself, 'This is scary, but I can handle scary,' and I keep my voice steady. The more grounded I feel, the less trapped I am by what I'm seeing.
In the rewrite I don't fight the fear so hard—I just notice it and let it pass through me. That takes away the frozen feeling, and I can think clearly again.
I put my hand over my reflection and imagine warm golden light pouring out of it, sealing everything back together. My skin smooths out and the mirror can't distort me anymore.
I turn into a stronger version of myself, almost like armor grows over me, so the melting can't touch me. The reflection loses its creepy smile when it sees I changed too.
I realize I can use magic in the dream, so I snap my fingers and the mirror turns into harmless steam. Without it there, the whole nightmare just dissolves.
I stop looking at the mirror and just stare at the floor, trying not to move at all. I figure if I stay perfectly still, maybe it won't get worse.
In the rewrite, I crouch down under the sink cabinet and make myself small until the buzzing light and the mirror are out of sight. I just wait there for it to pass.
I put my hands over my face and back into the corner of the bathroom. I don't try to fix anything, I just shut down and hope the reflection leaves me alone.
I tell myself to wake up right then and yank myself out of the dream before my face melts any further. The whole goal is just to get out.
I pinch myself hard in the dream and use that to wake up. I don't stay with the scene long enough for anything to change.
I imagine hitting some kind of off switch and the bathroom just goes black so I can wake up in bed. I basically end the dream instead of dealing with it.
I grab something heavy and beat the mirror over and over until it's shattered and the smiling reflection is gone. I keep hitting it even after it's already broken.
I set the bathroom on fire and watch the mirror, the sink, all of it melt down worse than my face did. I want to destroy everything in there so nothing survives.
I reach through the glass, drag the thing smiling at me out, and tear it apart with my hands. It's not enough to stop it, I want to mutilate it completely.
In the new version I just shrug and tell myself it doesn't bother me. My face can melt and I feel basically nothing about it.
I stand there and say I'm fine, like none of it is upsetting at all. I don't let myself react emotionally to the smell or what I see in the mirror.
I rewrite it so I'm just flat and detached, almost bored by it. I keep telling myself there's no fear, no disgust, nothing really happening inside me.
Honestly, it just plays out the same way. I look in the mirror, my face starts sliding off, and I can't change any of it.
The rewrite is basically no rewrite—I'm back in that bathroom with the buzzing light, holding my face while it dissolves in my hands. The reflection still smiles at me at the end.
I just relive the whole thing beat for beat, with the dripping sound, the burnt smell, and my mouth stretching open. Nothing shifts or gets resolved; it happens exactly like before.
I feel pure panic, like I’m trapped in my own body and can’t do anything except watch it happen. It’s this sick, helpless terror.
I’m horrified and disgusted at the same time. It feels violating, and I’m completely helpless in that moment.
It’s just dread, really—heavy, paralyzing dread. I feel scared down to my stomach and almost numb with it.
The bathroom is dim and washed out, with that harsh fluorescent light flickering overhead. Everything feels cold, stale, and too quiet except for the buzzing.
The mirror is smeared and the sink below it catches this slow, wet dripping sound. The whole space feels claustrophobic and unclean.
The air smells burnt and sweet in a nauseating way. The light keeps flickering, and the room has this unreal, grimy feeling to it.
I slam my fist into the mirror over and over to stop that smiling reflection and keep it from coming any closer. I’m just trying to make it stop, but I hit as hard as I can until the glass gives way.
I just stand there shaking, staring at my face coming apart, and I keep saying that I’m scared and can’t do anything. It feels like all I can do is admit how terrified I am.
I tell myself to stay calm and not make a big deal out of it, like if I keep it together the melting can’t really get to me. I kind of push the panic down and focus on getting through it.
It’s the same bathroom, the same buzzing light, and my face starts sliding off in the mirror exactly the way it always does. I just watch it happen again from the same spot.
I pull myself away from the sink and move fast toward the door, just trying to get out of the mirror’s view. It feels like I’m doing something, but mostly I need distance from it.
